Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the new Central Library. My name's Tom, and I'm going to tell you a little about the building before you explore it yourselves.

The library opened in March, two months later than planned, because of problems with the glass roof. It cost twelve million pounds. Local businesses gave some of the money, but most of it came from the city council.

The first thing most visitors notice is the light. The architects wanted the building to feel like being outdoors, so the roof is made almost entirely of glass, and there are trees growing inside the main hall.

Membership is free for everyone who lives or studies in the city. You don't need a passport or a photo; you just need to show a document with your address, such as a bank statement. You can borrow up to twelve items at a time, for three weeks.

Now, the floors. On the ground floor, you'll find the café and the children's library, which has a special storytelling corner. The first floor is where most of our books for adults are, and it also has the music room, where you can book a soundproof studio to practise an instrument.

The second floor is our quiet floor: no phones, no talking, just individual study desks. And at the top, on the third floor, there's the local history archive, with old maps and newspapers going back two hundred years, and a roof terrace with views over the river.
A few practical things. The library opens at eight in the morning on weekdays and at ten at weekends. We close at eight every evening, except on Sundays, when we close at five.

Agreed. Oh, and we need a short video. Shall we both film something?
Let's ask Mr Díaz first whether videos count toward the time limit. If they do, we might not have space.
Good point. The limit's fifteen minutes, isn't it?
Right. I think the hardest part is explaining why people don't recycle more.

I partly agree, but I also think many people simply don't know which plastics can be recycled.
Then maybe that's our main recommendation: clearer labels on packaging.
Yes, that's practical. Let's meet on Friday to put it all together.

Today I want to talk about one of the most remarkable journeys in nature: bird migration. Every year, about four thousand species of birds, roughly forty per cent of all species, travel between the places where they breed and the places where they spend the winter. Colombia is an important stop for many of them: more than a hundred and fifty migrant species spend the northern winter here.

Why do birds migrate? The main reason is food. In the northern summer, days are long and insects are plentiful, which is perfect for raising chicks. When winter comes, food becomes scarce, so birds fly south, where it is still available.

The distances can be extraordinary. The Arctic tern holds the record: it flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, a round trip of about seventy thousand kilometres. Smaller birds are just as impressive. The blackpoll warbler, which weighs only twelve grams, flies non-stop over the Atlantic Ocean for up to three days.

How do they find their way? Scientists believe birds use several methods together. Young birds seem to be born with a sense of direction. They also use the position of the sun during the day and the stars at night. Perhaps most surprisingly, many birds can sense the Earth's magnetic field, rather like a compass. In one experiment, pigeons carrying small magnets found their way less accurately on cloudy days, when they could not see the sun.
Preparing for migration takes a great deal of energy. Before leaving, many birds eat so much that they almost double their body weight, storing the extra energy as fat.

Unfortunately, migration is becoming more dangerous. The biggest threat is the loss of habitat, especially the wetlands and forests where birds stop to rest and feed. City lights are another problem: they confuse birds that fly at night, and millions die every year after hitting glass buildings. In the next lecture, we'll look at how scientists track individual birds using tiny GPS devices.

Today we're going to look at the history of chocolate. Chocolate comes from the seeds of the cacao tree, which grows naturally in the tropical forests of Central and South America. In fact, recent research in Ecuador suggests that people were using cacao more than five thousand years ago.

The Maya, and later the Aztecs, prepared cacao as a drink, not as a solid food. It was bitter, not sweet, and was often mixed with chilli and maize. Cacao beans were so valuable to the Aztecs that they were used as money: a rabbit, for example, could cost about ten beans.
When the Spanish brought cacao to Europe in the sixteenth century, Europeans added sugar to make the drink sweeter, and it became fashionable among rich people.

The big change came in the nineteenth century. In 1828, a Dutch chemist invented a machine that pressed the fat, called cocoa butter, out of the beans, leaving a powder that was easier to mix. This made it possible, in 1847, for a British company to make the first chocolate bar.

Today, most of the world's cacao is grown not in the Americas but in West Africa, especially in Ivory Coast and Ghana. Many cacao farmers earn very little, which is why some consumers choose chocolate with a fair trade label.

Today let's look at how honeybees share information about food. When a worker bee finds a good source of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs what's called a waggle dance. She moves in a straight line while shaking her body, then circles back and repeats.

The direction of the straight line tells the other bees where the food is, relative to the sun. So if she dances straight up the honeycomb, the food is in the direction of the sun. And the length of the waggle tells them how far away it is: a longer waggle means a greater distance.
This was worked out by Karl von Frisch, who later won a Nobel Prize for it. What's remarkable is that bees adjust the dance as the sun moves across the sky during the day.

In the 1880s, a German psychologist named Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory by learning lists of nonsense syllables. He found that he forgot most of a list within a day, a pattern now called the forgetting curve.

But he also found something useful. If he reviewed a list several times with gaps in between, he remembered it much longer than if he studied it many times in one session. This is known as the spacing effect. Modern studies confirm it: students who spread their study over several days usually do better than students who study the same amount the night before.

Why does it work? One explanation is that each time we nearly forget something and then recall it, the memory becomes stronger. So, for your own exams, a little practice every day is better than one long session.

In the middle, a boy is cutting vegetables, maybe carrots. On the right, a girl is putting plates on the table. It looks like they're preparing dinner together, and they all seem happy and relaxed.

I'd like to talk about the time I helped my neighbour, an old man who lives alone. Last year he broke his leg, so for about a month I did his shopping every Saturday and sometimes stayed to chat with him. I felt really good, because he was so grateful and he told me amazing stories about his life. I think people volunteer because it makes them feel useful and connected to others, and sometimes because they remember a time when someone helped them. As for schools, I think volunteer work should be encouraged, but maybe not compulsory. If students are forced to do it, they might not care, but if schools offer interesting projects and give students a choice, many of them would take part and learn a lot.

At weekends I like to relax, so on Saturday mornings I usually sleep a bit later. In the afternoon I play football with my friends in the park near my house, and on Sundays we often visit my grandparents and have a big lunch together.

This picture shows an outdoor market on a sunny day. There are two stalls with colourful awnings, and they're selling different kinds of fruit, like oranges and grapes. Behind the stalls I can see two sellers. In the front, a woman is walking with a child and carrying a shopping bag. It looks like a busy, friendly place, maybe on a weekend morning.

Both pictures show young people in their free time, but they're very different. In the first one, three teenagers are playing football in a park on a sunny day. In the second one, a teenager is sitting alone on a bed at night, playing a video game. The first activity is outdoors and social, while the second is indoors and quite isolated.

I'd like to talk about when I learnt to swim, which was quite difficult for me. I was already eleven, and all my friends could swim, so I felt embarrassed. My uncle took me to the pool every Sunday for three months, and at first I was really scared of putting my face in the water. In the end, I managed to swim a whole length, and I felt incredibly proud. I think some people find it hard to learn new things because they're afraid of failing in front of others. As for teachers or the internet, I think it depends. The internet is great for information, but a good teacher notices your mistakes and motivates you, which is really important for difficult skills.

I live in an apartment on the fifth floor of a building in the north of the city. It's not very big, but it's bright and we have a small balcony where my mum grows plants. The best thing is the view of the mountains in the mornings.

I'd like to describe a park near the centre of my city that I really love. It's about ten minutes from my house by bike. I go there two or three times a week, usually in the late afternoon after school. There's a big lake in the middle, and a path around it where people run and walk their dogs. Most of the time I go with my friends; we sit on the grass, listen to music and talk about our plans. Sometimes I go alone with a book when I want some peace. The reason I like it so much is that it feels like a break from the noise of the city. There are lots of trees and birds, and even though it's in the middle of everything, it's quiet. It's also a place full of memories, because I learnt to ride a bike there when I was small.

I think people enjoy public places like parks because they offer something most homes don't have: space and nature. In big cities, many people live in small apartments, so a park is where they can exercise, let their children play or simply relax. Parks are also social spaces. You meet neighbours, see families having picnics, and feel part of a community, which is important in cities where people often feel isolated.
I'm a student. I'm in my last year of secondary school, and I'm hoping to study engineering at university next year. It's a busy year because we have the national exam, but I'm enjoying it.

I'd like to talk about my grandmother, who taught me how to cook. She lives in a small town a few hours from my city, and I used to spend every school holiday with her. She taught me to make traditional dishes, especially arepas and sancocho. She never used recipes; instead, she let me watch her, then try it myself, and she corrected me very patiently when I made mistakes. I remember burning the first arepas I made, and she just laughed and said we would try again the next morning. This was important to me for two reasons.
